implementation_notes: cattrs is the in-Python form of the pattern: one Converter object owns both directions (structure for data to object, unstructure for object to data) and per-type hooks registered with register_structure_hook/register_unstructure_hook - or generated with cattrs.gen - keep the mapping outside both the class and the wire format. The classic converter class is unnecessary while the two types stay unaware of each other; stdlib-only code writes the same pair as dataclass methods plus asdict, or subclasses json.JSONEncoder and passes object_hook to JSONDecoder.
code_sketch:
@define
class Ticket:
    id: int
    created_at: datetime

c = Converter()                                    # both directions, one registry
c.register_unstructure_hook(datetime, lambda d: d.isoformat())
c.register_structure_hook(datetime, lambda s, _: datetime.fromisoformat(s))

wire = c.unstructure(Ticket(1, datetime.now()))    # object -> data
ticket = c.structure(wire, Ticket)                 # data -> object
pitfalls: Hooks registered for a concrete class do not cover subclasses the way a naive reading suggests; register_structure_hook_func exists for structural matching.
unstructure returns primitives, not JSON: json.dumps still needs default= for anything the hooks left untouched.
Naive and aware datetime values survive a round trip as different objects, and fromisoformat-style parsing accepts both silently.
Attribute validators run during structure, not during direct construction, so objects created in code can violate the invariants the wire path enforces.

variants.name: dataclass with to_dict()/from_dict() pair (no dependency)
variants.implementation_notes: Without a library each dataclass owns its pair - a to_dict() method (or dataclasses.asdict for the shallow case) plus a from_dict() classmethod - which is the same contract cattrs would register, only spelled per type. This is the right shape while the wire format is a plain dict or JSON and the mapping is a handful of fields, and it should delegate value formatting to the value types themselves; it becomes a liability once several types share the same conventions, which is when a registry pays off.
pitfalls: asdict() recurses into nested dataclasses but does not convert non-JSON value types, so mixing it with explicit formatting yields two different wire shapes.
A from_dict that uses data.get() instead of key lookup turns a missing required field into a silent None.
The pair must be edited together: a field added to the dataclass without touching to_dict and from_dict keeps the old contract and no error is raised.
